The order stays put this week, and the story worth your attention is regulatory rather than product. The FDA's public safety notification on exosome products remains current as of May 2026, and it is unambiguous: administering unapproved exosome products to patients violates federal law. No exosome product has completed a full drug approval pathway. Enforcement now reaches manufacturers, distributors, clinic operators and the physicians who administer them.

Here is what that means for you, because the headline sounds scarier than the shelf reality. That notification targets injectables and clinical administration. Every product on this list is a topical serum you apply with your fingertips, which sits in cosmetics territory. The line the FDA draws is at structure and function claims. The moment a brand says its product regenerates skin or stimulates collagen, it has argued itself into drug classification regardless of how the product goes on. So read labels for what they promise, and treat the loud claims as a regulatory risk signal rather than a quality signal.

A Dermatological Reviews paper published this year names the real technical problem: cell sourcing, manufacturing and characterisation vary substantially between makers, which makes standardisation genuinely hard. Two serums both saying exosomes on the front can differ by orders of magnitude in particle count.

That variability is exactly why Plated Intense holds first. Exosome count and manufacturing consistency are the two things it publishes and can defend, and its 9.6 efficacy score reflects documented potency rather than a number I inferred.

Plated's platelet derived exosome platform has published trial data on wrinkle appearance and skin texture, and in a category where most marketing rests on mechanism stories rather than outcomes, that difference decides the ranking.

Cell Forté holds second and Exocel Bio's EXO ELITE sits third, both with credible formulation work and reasonable transparency about exosome source and concentration.

I want to give an honest framing of this category because the price points demand it. Exosome serums are the most expensive skincare most people will ever consider, and the evidence base, while real, is early. What is well established is that they are generally well tolerated and that the delivery vehicles are usually excellent, which means part of what you feel is a very good serum base doing familiar work.

My practical advice: use it as a post procedure product where the case is strongest, which is after microneedling or laser when barrier recovery is what you want. For daily anti ageing on intact skin, a well formulated retinoid and a daily sunscreen deliver more measured benefit per dollar than anything in this category. That is not a knock on these products. It is a statement about where the strongest evidence sits.
